content: The 2011 study conducted in the USA was a randomized controlled trial set in an inner-city prenatal care clinic in Michigan. The study included pregnant women aged 18 to 45 with at least one month of expected gestation remaining. Participants needed to understand spoken English and meet one of the following criteria: (1) problem alcohol use as defined by T-ACE criteria, (2) exceeding the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) sensible drinking limits before pregnancy (more than seven standard drinks per week or more than two drinks at a time), or (3) reporting alcohol consumption at least once per month during pregnancy. Exclusion criteria included psychosis, intoxication, cognitive impairment, inability to communicate in English, or lack of access to a phone for follow-up. The intervention group received software-tailored content based on their current drinking status, including personalized feedback and discussions about the pros and cons of quitting alcohol. Participants were also asked about their interest in quitting. The control group answered questions about TV shows and videos of popular entertainers, followed by subjective preference ratings. The duration of the control group activities matched that of the intervention group. Alcohol consumption was measured post-intervention in terms of frequency, quantity, and binge use. Ethical approval was obtained from Wayne State University Institutional Review Board and the Detroit Medical Center Research Review Committee. Participants provided signed informed consent. The study was funded by an NIAAA training grant (AA16256). The 2003 study by Whaley was a cluster randomized trial conducted in the USA at Public Health Foundation Enterprises (PHFE) WIC centers in Los Angeles and Orange counties. The trial lasted 25 months, from May 2000 to May 2002. Twelve of the 53 PHFE-WIC sites were randomly selected to administer a self-report alcohol screening tool to all pregnant women, while the remaining 41 sites continued standard WIC care. For analysis, 12 control sites were matched to the intervention group based on caseload size, Hispanic population size, maternal age, and maternal education. The intervention used an alcohol screening tool incorporating quantity-frequency measures and the Time-Line Followback method. Quantity-frequency measures assessed typical drinking patterns, including the amount consumed on an average day and the frequency of alcohol use. The Time-Line Followback method provided a detailed picture of drinking behavior over specific time periods and has been extensively validated in clinical and non-clinical populations. Maternal outcomes included ongoing substance use during pregnancy, while no infant outcomes were reported. The evidence from various studies suggests that psychosocial interventions, such as motivational interviewing (MI), cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), and contingency management (CM), have varying levels of effectiveness in addressing substance use during pregnancy. MI has not demonstrated superiority over treatment-as-usual or educational controls in terms of maternal retention in treatment or substance use reduction. CBT has shown potential benefits, including improved treatment retention, reduced risk behaviors, and lower rates of preterm birth. CM has been found to be superior to treatment-as-usual in terms of treatment retention, negative urine tests, and continuous abstinence from cocaine. However, home visits have not been effective in reducing maternal retention in treatment, substance use, or alcohol use. Educational and counseling interventions may encourage women to reduce or cease alcohol use during pregnancy. Psychosocial interventions for substance use and co-occurring mental disorders in non-pregnant populations are well-supported by research, and retention in substance abuse treatment is a critical factor in reducing illicit substance use. Potential harms of interventions include physical and mental symptoms associated with cessation or reduction of substance use, development of depression or anxiety, partner abuse, substitution of one substance for another, and stigmatization. Between 7% and 15% of individuals undergoing psychosocial interventions may experience a decline in functioning post-treatment due to factors such as lack of provider bonding, goal direction, monitoring, or high emotional arousal and stigma. Economic and time burdens, as well as conflicts with partners, family, or employers, may also arise. Despite these challenges, psychosocial interventions offer opportunities for positive behavior change, development of coping strategies, and potential reductions in community crime and sexually transmitted infection risks. However, stigma, disbelief in intervention effectiveness, and resource allocation concerns remain barriers to widespread implementation.
